title: Docker Volumes
subtitle: Persistent storage, bind mounts and backup
description: Containers are disposable; data is not. Learn when to use named volumes, bind mounts and tmpfs, and how to back up and restore safely.
outcomes: Choose the right mount type for each use case
Back up and restore a volume without downtime surprises

modules.title: Storage model
modules.summary: Where data lives and what survives.

lessons.title: Storage drivers, volumes and tmpfs
lessons.summary: The writable layer is disposable. Volumes are the supported persistence mechanism.
objectives: Explain the writable layer and its cost
Use tmpfs for ephemeral sensitive data

sections.title: Three places data can live
sections.body:
The **writable layer** is tied to the container and is removed with it. A **volume** is managed by Docker, stored outside the image layers, and can outlive containers. A **bind mount** maps an arbitrary host path into the container. `tmpfs` stores data in memory and disappears on stop.

Volumes are the default recommendation for databases and application state because Docker manages their lifecycle and they work on every platform.

sections.caption: Writable layer, named volume, bind mount and tmpfs compared.

sections.code:
docker volume create app-data
docker run -d --name db \
  -v app-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=example \
  postgres:16-alpine

docker volume inspect app-data
docker volume ls
docker volume rm app-data   # fails while in use

sections.title: Use --mount for clarity in automation
sections.body: `--mount type=volume,source=app-data,target=/data` is more explicit than `-v`, and it fails loudly when the source does not exist.

exercises.expected: docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16-alpine

exercises.prompt: Mount a tmpfs at /run/app for a container.

questions.question: What happens to the writable layer when a container is removed?
questions.explain: Only volumes and bind mounts persist.

questions.question: Which storage is removed on container stop?
questions.explain: tmpfs lives in memory for the container lifetime.

questions.question: Can you remove a volume that a container is using?
questions.explain: Docker protects in-use volumes; force removal is not the default.

lessons.title: Bind mounts and permissions
lessons.summary: Direct host paths are powerful for development and risky in production.
objectives: Use bind mounts for local development

sections.title: The host owns the files
sections.body:
A bind mount maps a host path directly. UIDs inside the container are the same numeric UIDs on the host unless user namespaces are enabled. That is the source of most "permission denied" errors: the container process runs as UID 1000 while the host directory is owned by UID 0 or another user.

Use bind mounts for source code in development, configuration files, and local tooling. Avoid them for production state; they couple the container to host layout and permissions.

sections.code:
# development source mount
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/app -w /app node:20-alpine sh

# read-only config
docker run -d -v "$PWD/nginx.conf":/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro nginx:alpine

# SELinux relabel (Linux)
docker run -d -v "$PWD/site":/usr/share/nginx/html:ro,Z nginx:alpine

# inspect the resolved mounts
docker inspect --format '{{json .Mounts}}' CONTAINER
sections.note: `-v` creates a host directory if it does not exist, which often hides typos. `--mount` requires the path to exist.

sections.title: Secrets and bind mounts
sections.body: A bind-mounted secret file is visible to the container and lives on the host. Set restrictive permissions and never mount a directory containing unrelated secrets.

exercises.title: Read-only config
exercises.prompt: Mount ./nginx.conf into the nginx config path read-only.

exercises.title: Fix ownership
exercises.prompt: A bind-mounted directory is not writable by UID 1000. Give two safe fixes.
exercises.expected: chown the host directory to UID 1000, or run the container with --user matching the host UID.

questions.question: Why do bind mounts cause permission errors?
options: Numeric UIDs are shared with the host
questions.explain: Container UIDs map to host UIDs unless user namespaces are used.

questions.question: What does the :ro suffix do?
questions.explain: The container cannot write to the mount.

questions.question: Which mount type is best for a production database?
options: Bind mount to a host directory
questions.explain: Named volumes are portable and Docker-managed.

lessons.title: Backup and restore volumes
lessons.summary: A repeatable tar-based backup, a restore drill, and what not to do with live database files.
objectives: Back up and restore a named volume

sections.title: Backup is a container that mounts two volumes
sections.body: The standard pattern runs a temporary container with the data volume mounted read-only and a backup directory mounted writable. `tar` writes an archive to the backup directory. No data is copied to the host filesystem unless the second mount is a bind mount.

sections.code:
# Backup
docker run --rm \
  -v app-data:/data:ro \
  -v "$PWD/backups":/backup \
  alpine sh -c 'tar czf /backup/app-data-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).tgz -C /data .'

# Restore into a fresh volume
docker volume create app-data-restore
docker run --rm \
  -v app-data-restore:/data \
  -v "$PWD/backups":/backup \
  alpine sh -c 'tar xzf /backup/app-data-20260101-1200.tgz -C /data'
sections.note: For a live database, stop writes or use the database native dump (pg_dump, mysqldump) for a consistent backup.

sections.title: Test restores
sections.body: An untested backup is a hypothesis. Restore into a throwaway volume and verify the application can read it before you need it.

exercises.title: Backup command
exercises.prompt: Write a tar backup of volume pgdata into ./backups.
exercises.expected: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data:ro -v "$PWD/backups":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data .

exercises.title: Restore drill
exercises.prompt: Restore that archive into a new volume and list the files.
exercises.expected: Create a new volume, mount it and the backup dir, run tar xzf, then ls.

questions.question: Why mount the data volume read-only during backup?
questions.explain: Read-only prevents the backup container from modifying data.

questions.question: What is the safest backup for a live Postgres database?
options: tar of the data directory while running
questions.explain: A filesystem copy of a live database can be inconsistent.

questions.question: Where does the backup file live in the example?
questions.explain: The second mount writes the archive to the host.
